extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, judges, and legal scholars (those construing or litigating patents)
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and standards for interpreting letters-patent (claims, specification, drawings, prosecution history) to determine the scope of the patented invention. Includes principles on liberal construction, limits of interpretation, use of extrinsic evidence (state of the art, file history), and how the whole patent is read together.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule of liberal construction in favor of the patentee
rubrics_metrics.description: A liberal construction is given to the patent when its terms are so interpreted as to sustain the patent and cause it to protect the actual invention; doubtful points must be resolved so as to support the patentee's claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply legitimate meanings to words/phrases that make the claim/description correspond to the essential characteristics of the true invention; courts recognize claims/descriptions may be unskilfully drawn and should be read liberally to secure the actual invention. (See §736 and multiple cited cases.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Liberal construction does not authorize changing patent language
rubrics_metrics.description: The rule of liberal construction does not permit courts to change the language of the patent or to give words wholly different meanings; courts cannot create new terms or a new specification by interpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the language is erroneous or the inventor discovered more than disclosed, remedy is amendment or new patent, not forced construction. Courts must interpret but not substitute or invent terms. (See §737.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims construed by their own language; clear claims control
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims must be construed by the language which is employed; when a claim is clear and explicit its language controls and need not be aided by other parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely on what might have been employed; treat clear claims as definitive. Only when claims are ambiguous should the specification and other parts be consulted. (See §737, §742.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation as a person skilled in the art would
rubrics_metrics.description: The court should interpret a patent as persons skilled in the art would, applying its words to its subject-matter in a practical, not fanciful, manner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep the construction consistent with the understanding of ordinary mechanics/technicians in the relevant art; avoid interpretations that would perplex an ordinary mechanic. (Cites: Tondeur v. Stewart; Davoll v. Brown.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction must not be elastic or ambiguous
rubrics_metrics.description: The rule of liberal construction does not permit interpretations that render claims elastic or ambiguous; interpretation aims to make the indefinite exact and the doubtful plain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use interpretative power to remove, not create, ambiguities; do not erect or destroy limitations arbitrarily. (See §738.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims cannot be enlarged by construction beyond explicit description
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent is not to be enlarged by construction beyond what is explicitly described and claimed; limited claims are not to be expanded into general ones by implication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not cover matter intentionally omitted or later inventions by construing claims broadly; if the patent does not cover something the patentee intended, the remedy is amendment, not construction. (See §737–§739.)

rubrics_metrics.name: No creation of new specification or substitution of terms by implication
rubrics_metrics.description: While courts may depart from literal import to avoid destroying the inventor's right, they cannot make new specifications by implication or interpolate terms not appearing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The court's duty is discharged when it defines the character of the invention according to the significance of words employed; it may not interpolate or exclude present terms to alter scope. (See §737.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent construed in light of the state of the art at date of invention
rubrics_metrics.description: The nature and scope of the invention are shown by the state of the art at the date of the invention; patents are to be construed in view of prior devices, knowledge, and human knowledge as of that date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine prior patents, processes, instruments, and testimony about the art's history and development to determine what was new and the precise step taken by the inventor; restrict general terms by prior art where appropriate. (See §740.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification and drawings used to construe claims when claims ambiguous
rubrics_metrics.description: When claims are obscure or capable of different constructions, the whole description, drawings, model, oath, and title should be considered as exponents and interpreters of the claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the specification as the inventor's own interpreter of claim meaning and essential qualities; be mindful that no descriptive portion controls others and that the specification should be read to learn what the patentees meant to claim. (See §742.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentee entitled to protection for all forms of his invention unless he restricted himself
rubrics_metrics.description: A patentee is entitled to such a construction as will enable the patent to protect all forms of his invention, even if he described but one, unless the claims restrict him to certain forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give effect to the manifest design and essential attributes of the invention to protect other forms that embody the same inventive principle, subject to the literal terms and any clear restrictions in the claims. (See §740.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of prosecution history and inventor's pre-grant statements
rubrics_metrics.description: The position assumed before the Patent Office — application, claims asserted, amendments, disclaimers, objections answered or avoided — are proper matters for examination in construing the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine correspondence, file history, and concessions made to the Patent Office; a patentee cannot later insist the patent covers matter he was compelled to abandon. Rejected applications and amendments may limit scope. Post-issue statements by the inventor have little weight. (See §741.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Entire patent construed together as an indivisible instrument
rubrics_metrics.description: In ascertaining the purpose of the patent, the entire patent must be construed together and effect given to all its parts (claims, specification, drawings, model, oath, title) as members of a single instrument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When claims are ambiguous, look through the whole patent to ascertain what is claimed; no one descriptive part may unilaterally control others. (See §742 and multiple case citations.)

rubrics_metrics.name: When language is clear, follow literal meaning even if patent fails to cover actual invention
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the language of a patent is clear and capable of only one meaning, the court must define the invention according to that interpretation even if the patent thereby does not protect the patentee's broader actual invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If clear language would do violence to the terms employed, a different interpretation may be necessary; otherwise the inventor must amend or accept the consequences. (See §739.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Details and peculiarities are not essential unless claimed or described as such
rubrics_metrics.description: Peculiarities of shape or arrangement, or mere details recommended in the description, are not to be construed as essential features of the invention unless the description or claim suggests them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not construe non-essential details as distinct limitations to save a claim; only features expressly or clearly indicated as essential should limit claim scope. (See §738.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims for special arrangements limited to those special parts and arrangement
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim that is for the special arrangement of parts must be construed to cover only the special parts and special arrangement described.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not treat a claim to a particular arrangement as a broad claim to the general idea; construction must respect the specificity of such claims. (See §739.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentee's own contemporaneous interpretation is persuasive if consistent with language
rubrics_metrics.description: The construction given to the patent by the patentee will be sustained if it is consistent with the language used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defer to the patentee's reasonable interpretation from his submissions and conduct if such interpretation aligns with the patent text; but acquiescence or file-history limitations may restrict later contentions. (See citations: Tondeur v. Stewart; Winans v. Denmead.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Patents are construed in view of human knowledge — not as intending impossibilities
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification will be construed in view of the state of human knowledge and not as intending the impossible; the description is limited by what appears new in the art at the invention date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid construing disclosures as claiming more than what contemporary knowledge made possible; restrict claims consistent with the art's capabilities at that time. (See §740.)

rubrics_metrics.name: No construction can supply what the inventor deliberately omitted or was denied in prosecution
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims may not be construed to cover matter the patentee intentionally omitted or was forced to abandon in the Patent Office; acquiescence in rejection restricts later claim breadth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The records of the Patent Office (applications, rejections, amendments) may be examined, and an assignee cannot expand scope to cover matter excluded by claim allowance/rejection. (See §741–§742.)
